content.title: Pronoun Case and Pronoun Reference
content.overview: This lesson focuses on selecting the correct pronoun form based on its grammatical role in a sentence and ensuring that every pronoun has a clear, logical antecedent.
learning_objectives: Identify the grammatical role of a pronoun as a subject, object, or reflexive element.
Select the correct pronoun case (subjective, objective, or reflexive) for compound structures.
Apply the substitution method to verify pronoun case in complex phrases.
Ensure pronouns have clear and unambiguous references to specific nouns.

sections.title: Understanding Pronoun Case
sections.content: Pronoun case refers to the form a pronoun takes depending on its function in a sentence. There are three primary cases: 1. Subjective Case (I, he, she, we, they, who): Used when the pronoun is the subject performing the action. 2. Objective Case (me, him, her, us, them, whom): Used when the pronoun receives the action or follows a preposition (e.g., 'to,' 'with,' 'between'). 3. Reflexive Case (myself, himself, herself, ourselves, themselves): Used only when the subject and the object of the sentence are the same person or for emphasis.

sections.title: The Substitution Strategy for Compounds
sections.content: ACT questions often hide pronoun errors within compound phrases (e.g., 'my brother and I' vs. 'my brother and me'). To determine the correct case, temporarily remove the other person from the compound and read the sentence with only the pronoun. For example, in the sentence 'The teacher gave the books to Sarah and (I/me),' remove 'Sarah and.' You would say 'The teacher gave the books to me,' not 'to I.' Therefore, 'me' is the correct objective case.

sections.title: Pronouns After Prepositions
sections.content: A common trap involves prepositions like 'between,' 'among,' or 'with.' Pronouns following these must always be in the objective case. A frequent error is the phrase 'between you and I.' Because 'between' is a preposition, it requires the objective 'me,' making 'between you and me' the only correct form.

sections.title: Pronoun Reference Clarity
sections.content: A pronoun must refer clearly to one specific noun, known as the antecedent. If a sentence contains two possible nouns a pronoun could represent, or if the pronoun refers to a vague idea rather than a specific noun, it is a 'vague pronoun' error. On the ACT, you must choose the option that clarifies the identity of the pronoun, often by replacing the pronoun with a specific noun.

worked_examples.question: Choose the best revision for the underlined portion: 'The manager invited my supervisor and I to the annual luncheon.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the role: The pronoun is part of the compound object receiving the action 'invited.' 2. Use substitution: Remove 'my supervisor and.' The sentence becomes 'The manager invited I.' 3. Evaluate: 'Invited I' is incorrect; it should be 'invited me.' 4. Correct form: 'The manager invited my supervisor and me.'

worked_examples.question: Identify the error: 'After the students met with the advisors, they were relieved.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Check for clarity: Who does 'they' refer to—the students or the advisors? 2. Identify the ambiguity: The pronoun 'they' has two potential antecedents. 3. Fix: Replace 'they' with a specific noun, such as 'the students were relieved' or 'the advisors were relieved,' to ensure the meaning is clear.

common_mistakes: Using 'myself' to sound more formal when 'me' or 'I' is required (e.g., 'He gave it to myself' is incorrect).
Using the subjective case 'I' in a compound object (e.g., 'between you and I').
Assuming a pronoun is correct just because it is plural, without checking if the antecedent is clear.
exam_tips: If you see 'between' or 'among,' look for the objective case (me, him, her, us, them).
When a sentence has two people mentioned (like 'John and I'), always cross out the first person to test the pronoun alone.
If an answer choice replaces a pronoun with a specific noun, check if the original pronoun was vague; the specific noun is often the correct ACT answer.
content.recap: To master pronoun usage, identify if the pronoun is a subject or an object. Use the substitution method for compounds by testing the pronoun in isolation. Always ensure every pronoun points to one clear, specific noun to avoid reference errors.

knowledge_claims.content: The subjective case (I, he, she, we, they) is used when the pronoun acts as the subject of a verb.
The objective case (me, him, her, us, them) is used when the pronoun is the direct object, indirect object, or object of a preposition.
Pronouns following the preposition 'between' must always be in the objective case (e.g., 'between you and me').
To test a pronoun in a compound phrase, remove the other noun/pronoun and read the sentence with the remaining pronoun alone.
It is incorrect to use a reflexive pronoun like 'myself' if the subject of the sentence is not also the object.
A pronoun reference error occurs when a pronoun could logically refer to more than one noun in the sentence.
The pronouns 'who' and 'whom' follow case rules: 'who' is subjective and 'whom' is objective.
If a pronoun sounds correct in a compound but incorrect when used alone (e.g., 'for I'), the compound is grammatically wrong.
Reflexive pronouns should only be used for self-directed actions (e.g., 'I hurt myself') or for emphasis (e.g., 'I did it myself').
A pronoun must have a specific noun as an antecedent; it cannot vaguely refer to an entire preceding clause or idea.
Subjective pronouns perform actions, while objective pronouns receive actions or follow prepositions.
In the phrase 'my friend and me,' 'me' is objective; in 'my friend and I,' 'I' is subjective.

ENGLISH PASSAGE 1: The Clock Above Alder Street
[1] After three months of fundraising [[a neighborhood restoration crew began]] to repair the brass clock above Alder Street Market. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a market hall built in 1911, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] wear marks showed that an earlier repairer had reversed two nearly identical wheels. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because replacement parts would have erased those clues. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the crew cleaned and reused the original wheels. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the clock kept accurate time through a week of rain. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.]]

Which replacement for the pronoun marked [5] makes the reference clearest?
items.explanation: Repeating 'the visitors' removes the ambiguity about who asked the questions.

ENGLISH PASSAGE 2: Counting After Dark
[1] After several cloudy evenings [[a coastal ecology class began]] to count juvenile crabs in tide pools after sunset. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a protected inlet beside the school, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] the smallest crabs appeared most often under flat stones near eelgrass. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because bright white light changed the animals’ movement. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the class switched to dim red lamps and repeated the first survey. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the second set of counts was more consistent. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the revised method gave park staff a dependable baseline for future surveys.]]

Which replacement for the pronoun marked [5] makes the reference clearest?
items.explanation: Repeating 'the visitors' removes the ambiguity about who asked the questions.

videoLesson.title: Verify Pronoun Case and Reference
videoLesson.description: You will recognize a pronoun's grammatical role and its antecedent in a sentence. Label subject/object/prepositional roles and substitute the single pronoun to pick subjective, objective, or reflexive case.
